--- title: "Posteriors and bootstraps" description: "The Bayesian, Poisson and classical bootstraps of the universal model, exact in one pass or Gaussian from the compressed rows." order: 3 jupyter: python3 --- The product manager of the [Bayesian universal model post](https://jeffwong.github.io/posts/bayesian_universal_model/) asks: what is the probability that the setting cuts rebuffers per play by at least 10% for the profiles that use it? A standard error does not answer that. A posterior does. A bootstrap draw is the universal model refit with one more weight per cluster, $\xi_a^{(b)}$. The draw recomputes the propensities, $\hat\beta$ and $\bar x_C$. The three bootstraps differ only in how the weights are drawn: | `weights=` | $\xi_a$ | the draws are | |---|---|---| | `"bayesian"` | Exp(1) | a posterior (Dirichlet(1, …, 1) over the clusters) | | `"poisson"` | Poisson(1) | a sampling distribution | | `"multinomial"` | counts of $G$ draws with replacement | the classical bootstrap of clusters | Each weight is a pure function of (seed, cluster, draw), from a Philox stream, so it does not depend on row order or sharding. ::: {#bf403ccd .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import numpy as np import ume from ume.testing import simulate_accounts df = simulate_accounts(20_000, seed=2026) exp = ume.annotate( df, cluster="account", instrument="Z", treatment="T", cohort="day", covariates=ume.covariates(x1=2.0, x2=2.0, kids=0, device=ume.categorical(reference="tv")), ).metrics(ume.mean("y", name="hours"), ume.ratio("N", "D", name="rebuffers_per_play")) fit = exp.fit() ``` ::: ## Exact, in one pass `exp.bootstrap()` reads the rows once and builds every draw's sums at the same time: ::: {#98c2e4ca .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} post = exp.bootstrap(1000, weights="bayesian", seed=1) post ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ```{=html}

They also carry the uncertainty in $\hat e$ and $\bar x_C$, which the sandwich holds fixed: ::: {#afbaadad .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} fit.effects(se=post) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: ## From the compressed rows, with no pass Given the data, a stratum's weighted sum $\sum_{a \in h} \xi_a v_a$ has mean $\sum v_a$ and covariance $\sum v_a v_a^\top$: exactly the compressed row. `cd.posterior()` draws each stratum's sum from that normal distribution and refits each draw exactly: ::: {#883a2ab8 .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} cd = exp.compress() cd.posterior(1000, seed=1) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=5} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: It agrees with the exact posterior here, because every stratum has hundreds of clusters. With small strata (fewer than 200 clusters) it warns and recommends the exact engine: the normal multipliers can be negative, and small strata then widen and skew the posterior. ## The posterior agrees with the sandwich To first order, a draw moves an effect by $\sum_a (\xi_a - 1)\,\psi_a$ with independent weights of variance 1, so the posterior variance is close to the cluster sandwich: ::: {#7f5a792f .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} e = ume.Effect(exp.design.metrics[0]) { "sandwich SE": fit.effects().std_err("hours"), "posterior SD, exact": float(post.values(e).std(ddof=1)), "posterior SD, gaussian": float(cd.posterior(1000, seed=2).values(e).std(ddof=1)), "poisson bootstrap SD": float(exp.bootstrap(1000, weights="poisson", seed=3).values(e).std(ddof=1)), "classical bootstrap SD": float(exp.bootstrap(1000, weights="multinomial", seed=4).values(e).std(ddof=1)), } ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=6} ``` {'sandwich SE': 0.059260378704202234, 'posterior SD, exact': 0.05981242332877835, 'posterior SD, gaussian': 0.0612116588887785, 'poisson bootstrap SD': 0.06052751968494118, 'classical bootstrap SD': 0.05977992189008652} ``` ::: ::: ## The linearized standard error The bootstrap's first-order expansion has a closed form from the compressed rows: $\sum_h g_h^\top(\sum v_a v_a^\top)g_h$, with $g_h$ the gradient of the effect with respect to stratum $h$'s sums. Unlike the sandwich, it moves $\hat e$ and $\bar x_C$, so it tracks the posterior SD: ::: {#79ae8635 .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} fit.effects(se="linearized") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=7} ```{=html}
